To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the economic potential of microalga-based biofuel production is limited to ∼60 kl oil ha−2 y−1 (equivalent to 10 kl oil m−2 y−2) and that the maximum economic yield is achieved at an oil price of ∼$1,200 per ton.

the maximum sustainable yield of microalgal biodiesel is ∼60 to ∼100 kl oil ha-1 y-1 (∼6.600 to 10.800 gal ac-1 y- 1), and that the absolute theoretical ceiling of microalgal oil production is ∼94 to ∼155 kl oil ha- 1 y-1.

the theoretical yield of microalgae-based fuels is limited by the maximum theoretical photosynthetic efficiency of ∼10% and the practical yield is limited by the amount of sunlight available for biomass production.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the economic feasibility of microalgal systems for the production of biofuels, chemicals and food.
assessing the economic potential of microalga-based biofuel production systems.

the economic and technical feasibility of microalgal biodiesel production, and the potential for microalgae to provide a sustainable and cost-effective alternative to conventional petroleum-based diesel.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

microalgal oil production is economically feasible at a large scale and could become a significant source of renewable energy, but only when the technology has matured and the costs of production decrease.
microalgal biodiesel production systems are economically and technologically feasible and that the potential to displace petroleum-based fuels is significant.

the potential for large-scale microalgal bioenergy production is limited by the low solar conversion efficiency of photosynthesis, and that the most promising approach to achieve a sustainable and cost-effective biofuels supply is to integrate microalgal production with other industrial activities.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the current state-of-the-art for microalgal bioenergy production is economically and technically uncompetitive, but the technology is still in its infancy.
the current state-of-the-art in microalgal bioenergy research and development is still not sufficient to justify a significant investment in commercialization of the technology.
microalgal oil is a viable alternative to petroleum oil, but that its production cost is likely to be higher than that of conventional petroleum oil.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the current hype surrounding microalgal bioenergy technologies is largely unjustified, and the technology will only become economically viable when the cost of fossil fuels increases substantially.

microalgal biodiesel production will be limited by the availability of solar radiation and the photosynthetic conversion efficiencies that can be achieved by the microalgae, and not the cost of production, which is often cited by industry as the main barrier to the technology's widespread adoption.
microalgal systems are unlikely to be able to compete with conventional biofuel systems on a purely economic basis.
